title: When Speed of Response Becomes Your Security Nightmare
summary: Attacks are getting shorter, with some lasting as little as a few seconds. These short-duration DDoS attacks can slip through defenses, knock out a piece of infrastructure, or overwhelm an application.
body_markdown:
Recently, NETSCOUT observed a surge in attacks that manipulate timing to get around reactive defenses. Attacks are getting shorter, with some lasting as little as a few seconds. These short-duration distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks are designed to slip through defenses, knock out a piece of infrastructure, or overwhelm an application. Then, before automated defenses have a chance to react to them, they stop.


Knowing this is the case, why is DDoS still a problem for its victims? The answer lies with the attackers who are inventive, well-funded, and equipped with the latest technologies and tools to carry out their trade. They are mobile and constantly retool their attack arsenal to find holes in their victim’s defenses.


After attacks subside, the troubles aren’t over. In fact, they have just begun; cleanup and restoration are critical tasks. Systems have crashed, memory has run out, and recovery can take many minutes or even hours. For your company, every moment of downtime impacts your bottom line.


## Always-on Protection Is Needed


Years ago, a good response meant spotting an attack within six or seven minutes, and then getting a security team on it within another five or six. For an attack that might last hours, a 15-minute response time was viewed as rapid. More recently, automation has been developed to reduce the response times to minutes or in some cases less than a minute.


But according to NETSCOUT’S 1H 2026 DDoS Threat Intelligence[Report](https://www.netscout.com/threatreport/global-highlights/) , approximately seven in 10 attacks end within 15 minutes. Our 1H 2026[report](https://www.netscout.com/threatreport) found that attacks lasting a minute or less have nearly doubled their share of all attacks, from 1.6 percent in late 2023 to 3.1 percent in the first half of 2026. Attackers know defenses need time to kick in, so they are increasingly timing their strikes to hit before the response can stop them.


For businesses with little tolerance for downtime, leakage of attack traffic, even for short periods of time, is unacceptable. The bottom line is at stake. This shift to shorter-duration attacks means response times must also speed up to mitigate the damage, and there must be always-on defenses in place that provide constant protection.


## The Rising Cost of a Faster Opponent


These faster DDoS tactics carry real costs. For example, at a large retailer, application uptime is critical, and the losses stack up by the minute if there is downtime. Most companies can’t afford to be offline for a few minutes, let alone an hour.


In the case of a manufacturer, when systems go down, business stalls, inventory runs thin, and shortages show up right before the holiday season or a major brand launch. The results of these attacks show up on the balance sheet.


Reputation is another victim of attacks: Consider a government agency that goes off-line right before an election, or a university registrar that gets knocked offline during college enrollment time.


If this happens consistently, trust erodes. In the end, downtime is counted in lost users, and that loss lingers long after the servers come back online.


## Build the Sea Wall Before the Tsunami Hits


Coastal places such as Hawaii, Japan, and Indonesia know what the surge of water from a tsunami can do. I have previously referred to attacks above a terabit-per-second as internet tsunamis.


Much like sea walls built to stop the waves, businesses need to proactively build always-on security walls robust enough to absorb the DDoS surge the moment it hits. This buys time for smarter tools to do the finer work behind them.


Always-on means exactly that, running before an attack is launched. Some legitimate traffic may get caught, although customers will usually try again if they are momentarily blocked. The flip side is a site that stays down for minutes or hours. In those cases, companies rarely get a second chance from customers.


## The Wall Should Span Your Entire Network


An effective always-on wall should cover your entire network, whether it lives in the cloud, on your premises, or both. The important thing is to ensure that it is in-line and always vigilant. The cloud gives you sheer capacity. A big enough flood can clog the internet connection into your building, and then your application sits healthy but unreachable, with no customer able to get through.


A cloud service can absorb that flood before it arrives. Equipment in your own data center offers control. You can tune protection for each application and see exactly what is hitting each one. Most organizations need both, and the right mix depends on how much of the business runs online.


## The First Wave May Not Be the Last


Attacks are getting shorter and harder to pin down. NETSCOUT’s[1H 2026 DDoS Threat Intelligence Report](https://www.netscout.com/threatreport/) found that attacks lasting a minute or less doubled their share in six months, from 1.6 percent to 3.1 percent. The[2H 2025 report](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260304014007/en/netscout-reveals-qualitative-shifts-in-ddos-attack-sophistication-infrastructure-capacity-and-threat-actor-capabilities/) showed about 42 percent of attacks using two to five vectors at once, some adapting mid-attack. And NETSCOUT’s[ASERT researchers](https://www.netscout.com/blog/asert/when-chatbots-become-attack-coordinators-ai-revolution-ddos) say DDoS-for-hire services now offer automated scheduling and real-time adjustment, with AI taking over more of the coordination.


Withstanding the first wave of these attacks is the key to success. Once that is accomplished, additional defenses can be brought to bear, proactively tightening your defensive posture and ensuring that subsequent waves of attacks prove benign. Always-on protection is the best way to be prepared.
